summary: Examines address-scanning attacks in IPv6. The huge subnet size makes brute-force scanning look impractical, but this document discusses how attackers can still find hosts and what that means for security.

eli5.summary: Finding one house among a huge number of houses sounds impossible, but this shows there are still tricks to find them.

questions: how do attackers find hosts in ipv6
how to prevent ipv6 address scanning
what are low byte ipv6 addresses
subtitle: Why scanning an IPv6 subnet is harder than scanning IPv4, but far from impossible.

tldr.problem: IPv6 subnets are so large that brute-force address scanning looks impossible, which can give a false sense of safety.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC shows that real addresses follow predictable patterns that shrink the search space, describes scanning of remote and local networks, lists other ways to learn addresses, and gives mitigations.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational and obsoletes RFC 5157. Address scanning is less feasible than in IPv4 but may remain possible with good heuristics, so administrators should avoid predictable addressing.

today: RFC 7707 is an Informational RFC. It obsoletes RFC 5157, and the unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Scanning Is Not Hopeless
sections.content:
IPv6 has a much larger address space, so a typical IPv6 subnet has a far lower host density (hosts divided by addresses) than an IPv4 one. RFC 5157 argued that this makes classic network address scanning less feasible. This RFC, written with more than five years of IPv6 deployment experience, obsoletes it.

It stresses that address-scanning attacks are less feasible but may remain possible with appropriate heuristics, and that some classic address scanning has since been observed. It also covers other reconnaissance techniques. The RFC points out two sides of this: knowing the techniques can help administrators prevent or detect them, and reconnaissance is also essential for the penetration tests used to assess production networks.
sections.eli5: A town with billions of houses seems impossible to search. But people tend to pick house numbers that are easy to guess, so a clever searcher can still find them.

sections.title: How Address Patterns Shrink the Search Space
sections.content:
An IPv6 host address is usually a subnet prefix plus a 64-bit interface identifier (IID). How the IID is made decides how easy it is to guess.

  • SLAAC with IEEE identifiers: the IID is built from the MAC address with the fixed word 0xfffe inserted, and the first three bytes are a vendor OUI. The 64-bit space may drop to 2^24 or n * 2^24 for n OUIs. Virtual machines are worse: VirtualBox uses the OUI 08:00:27, giving 24 bits, and some VMware address schemes give 22 or 24 bits, or 8 bits when the console IPv4 address is known.
  • DHCPv6: servers that hand out addresses sequentially reduce the space to 8 or 16 bits. The RFC repeats the advice to issue random addresses from a large pool.
  • Manual addresses, common for routers and servers, tend to be low-byte, IPv4-based, service-port or wordy addresses such as 2001:db8::bad:cafe.
  • Privacy and opaque IIDs: temporary addresses and the stable, semantically opaque IIDs of RFC 7217 remove patterns, but temporary addresses are generated in addition to stable ones, so the stable address can still be scanned.

Measurements the RFC cites show that a very high share of host and router addresses follow specific patterns. Low-byte addresses were 56.88% of measured web servers and 92.65% of measured mail servers, while about 70% of measured clients appeared to use temporary addresses.
sections.eli5: If everyone at a school picks a locker number like 1, 2 or 3, you do not need to try every number to find a locker. Computers are often named in similarly lazy ways.

sections.title: Scanning Remote and Local Networks
sections.content:
Brute-forcing a whole /64 remotely is infeasible, so attackers are expected to use the patterns above. The RFC adds two points. Scanning a /64 could in theory create 2^64 entries in the last-hop router's Neighbor Cache, and some implementations cannot handle that, so a scan can become a denial of service. And a typical site with a /48 has up to 65,000 or so /64 subnets, but address plans (low numbers upward, building or VLAN numbers, or an IPv4 subnet number reused) can narrow that search too.

On a local network the job is much easier. An attacker can send probes to the all-nodes link-local multicast address ff02::1 to get replies from all local nodes. Windows systems do not answer multicast ICMPv6 Echo Requests, so tools also send packets with unrecognized options of type 10xxxxxx to trigger ICMPv6 Parameter Problem errors. Many tools find only link-local addresses, but probes sent with source addresses from different prefixes can help overcome that.
sections.eli5: Searching a faraway town house by house takes forever, but if you are standing in the school hall you can just shout and everybody answers.

sections.title: Other Ways to Learn IPv6 Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC lists many other methods, and marks which need local access or a login on a system. Without local access or login, attackers can use addresses published in DNS, DNS zone transfers, brute-forcing AAAA records against common host names, public mailing-list archives (the "Received from" headers), peer-to-peer applications, and traceroute6.

One DNS trick walks the ip6.arpa reverse zone. A PTR query returns an RCODE of 0 if there are hosts below that name and 4 (NXDOMAIN) if not, which greatly shrinks the search.

With local access or logins, the Neighbor Cache and routing table, configuration and log files (such as /etc/hosts or SSH known_hosts), routing protocols, IPFIX flow data, SNMP and plain traffic snooping all reveal addresses. Local name resolution and service discovery, such as mDNS and DNS-SD, are also sources. Worms could use some of these on a local network.
sections.eli5: Even if you hide your house number, people may still find it in a phone book, on an old letter or by asking the neighbors.

sections.title: Mitigations
sections.content:
The RFC gives a non-exhaustive list of ways to resist address scanning.

  • Use RFC 7217 stable, semantically opaque IIDs instead of addresses based on IEEE identifiers.
  • Use intrusion prevention systems at the perimeter and IPv6 packet filtering where applicable.
  • Use manually configured MAC addresses for virtual machines if scanning resistance matters.
  • Avoid sequential addresses in DHCPv6; allocate randomly from a large pool.
  • Keep the default /64 subnet size. Subnets of /112 or smaller are likely to make scanning more feasible.
  • In general, avoid being predictable in how addresses are assigned.

Two local vectors could be closed by not answering multicast ICMPv6 Echo Requests (already the default on Windows) and by making multicast packets never trigger ICMPv6 errors. The RFC adds that security by obscurity is not a defense in itself, and that on a local network other reconnaissance routes would remain.
sections.eli5: To stay hard to find, do not pick easy-to-guess numbers, and do not rely on being hidden as your only protection.

sections.title: Conclusions and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The conclusions say that the search space for address scanning is typically much smaller than the traditionally assumed 64 bits. They expect scanning to become more elaborate, and other reconnaissance techniques to be explored, as IPv6 deployment grows and more IPv6-only devices appear. Early dual-stack networks may be scanned over IPv4 first, but an IPv6 deployment with looser security policy may look like an easier target.

The Security Considerations section is short: because the document only reviews methods for finding host addresses within IPv6 subnets, it raises no new security concerns.
sections.eli5: The big lesson is that a huge number of houses does not make you safe if your house number is easy to guess.
